newsitem.title: CANADA: Toyota says magnesium price must fall.
newsitem.headline: Toyota says magnesium price must fall.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp said there has to be a notable decline in the price of magnesium before the Asian auto sector will consume significantly higher quantities of the light metal.
Board member Akiyoshi Morita told delegates at the World Magnesium Conference that magnesium prices have to fall to the same level as aluminum. "I believe this is possible," he said.
Magnesium is about twice the price of its sister light metal.

Toyota consumes 3,000 tonnes of magnesium a year. If the cost of magnesium fell to 1.5 times that of aluminum, Toyota would be expected to consume 10,000 tonnes a year, rising to 55,000 tonnes if magnesium and aluminum prices were the same, Morita said.
Magnesium is widely seen as a good candidate for components to make cars lighter, but has to compete against steel, aluminum and plastic.

Commenting on the speech, Robert Edgar, vice president of marketing at producer Hydro Magnesium, part of Norway's Norsk Hydro, said: "I don't think it's realistic to have magnesium price the same price as aluminium this decade or in the next."
"The cost comparison with aluminum is often the key point of debate of magnesium introduction," Morita said.
Magnesium was too expensive and usage in Japanese cars will barely change from present levels over the next few years, he added.
Magnesium also has to overcome some strength and corrosion issues, Morita said.

Japan has to import its magnesium, but in the U.S., where there is a large production base, the price of the metal is cheaper. Japanese original equipment manufacturers are also using highly engineered steel parts to cut car weight.
Japanese cars contain about 0.25 kilogram of magnesium each, compared to more than 1.5 kg in the U.S.
Elsewhere in Asia, China is expected to use more magnesium in cars parts.
Morita declined to answer directly a suggestion that Toyota makes magnesium car components in the U.S. where the metal is cheaper than in Japan.
